Get free greyhound racing tips and predictions for today's UK meetings from OLBG tipsters, with the most-tipped dog in each race and the reasoning behind the picks. Our coverage runs all year, from the daily graded cards to the sport's biggest open races.

For the classics, see our Greyhound Derby tips, Greyhound Oaks tips and Greyhound St Leger preview. Further down the page, you'll find track-by-track trap and favourite stats. For tips across every sport, visit our main betting tips page.
How Our Greyhound Racing Tips Work

Each day, this page shows the most popular free greyhound racing tips and predictions from OLBG members for today's UK meetings.

Every race listed above shows the most-tipped dog, its current odds, how many win tips it has received and its share of the tips in that race. The star value rating compares the dog's odds with its chance of winning as implied by that share of the tips, so the more stars, the more generous the price looks against the weight of tipping support.

To back a selection, use the Add button to put it straight into your betslip, or click through to the race page for the full picture on every runner.

Greyhound racing runs from late morning to late evening, with races only minutes apart, so it's easy to bet more often than you intended. Set a budget before you start, stick to races you've studied, and never chase losses. Betting is for over-18s only. If gambling stops being fun, free and confidential support is available from GamCare and GambleAware.

New to betting on the dogs? Our greyhound betting advice guide covers the basics.
How to Find Today's Greyhound Tips Race by Race

Click on any race above to open its race page. There you'll see two headline picks: the ‘Most Popular Tip’, which is the dog with the most tips from OLBG members, and the ‘Best Tipsters Tip’, which is the pick backed by the tipsters with the strongest greyhound records.

Below those, every runner is listed with its tips and the comments behind them. Each tip shows the tipster's greyhound profit and strike rate, so you can judge how much weight to give each prediction.

If you'd rather follow individual tipsters than individual races, see the full rankings on our best greyhound tipsters page.

How greyhound races are graded

Graded races make up most of the daily cards. Each race carries a letter for its distance category and a number for its class, with 1 the highest grade (so A1 is stronger than A5). The most common prefixes you'll see on a racecard are:

PrefixRace type
AStandard-distance graded race
DSprint
SStayers
EMarathon
PPuppy race
OROpen race, where dogs are selected on merit rather than by grade

Traps, reserves and jacket colours

British greyhound races have a maximum of six runners, one from each trap. If a dog is withdrawn through injury or illness, a reserve can take its place when a suitable one is available. Reserves are marked with an ‘R’ on the racecard and on their racing jacket.

Each trap has its own jacket colour:

  • Trap 1: Red
  • Trap 2: Blue
  • Trap 3: White
  • Trap 4: Black
  • Trap 5: Orange
  • Trap 6: Black and white stripes
Major Greyhound Races Our Tips Cover

Greyhound Derby

The English Greyhound Derby is the sport's flagship event, run over 500m with heats through May and the final in early June. Wimbledon hosted it from 1985 to 2016, before the track closed the following year. Since then it has been staged at Towcester, apart from 2019 and 2020 when Nottingham took over. Irish-trained runners have dominated recent renewals, as the table below shows. For heat-by-heat analysis, see our Greyhound Derby preview.

Greyhound St Leger

The St Leger is the premier staying classic. Like its horse racing namesake, it's a test for the stayers, and it's now run over 715m at Dunstall Park, with the final usually in September. Wembley, Wimbledon, Perry Barr and Nottingham have all hosted it in the past. Trainer Mark Wallis has an outstanding record in the race, with multiple wins since 2009. Read our Greyhound St Leger betting guide for the full preview.

Essex Vase

Run at Romford over 575m, the Essex Vase is one of the major six-bend competitions of the year. Its heats usually open the calendar in January, with the final in late January or early February. Ballyregan Bob, one of the sport's all-time greats, won it in 1985 and set a track record in the process, and Mark Wallis has won it a record six times.

TV Trophy

The TV Trophy is the leading marathon event of the year. It moves between tracks and is run over the host track's marathon trip, with recent renewals staged at Oxford and Towcester. It takes its name from the BBC, which televised it from 1958 until 1996. The most celebrated winner is Scurlogue Champ, who won in 1985 and 1986. He was famous for starting slowly and then cutting through the field with a devastating finish, which made him a huge crowd favourite. Among current trainers, Mark Wallis and Paul Young have each won it five times.

What trap number wins most often in greyhound racing?

With six runners, each trap would win around 16.7% of the time if the draw made no difference. In practice, the figures vary from track to track depending on the shape of the circuit and the run to the first bend. A trap that wins well above that baseline at a particular track may point to a draw bias worth factoring into your selections.

The chart below shows the win percentage for each trap at every GBGB track we cover in 2025. This is the share of runners from that trap that went on to win. The number beside each track name is the number of races included.

The strongest biases in 2025 were towards the wide draw at Harlow, where Trap 6 won 23.3% of the time, and the inside draw at Towcester, where Trap 1 won 23.0%. Trap 1 also did well at Hove, Dunstall Park and Sheffield, while Trap 6 stood out at Doncaster and Valley. Small samples, such as Dunstall Park in its first months, should be treated with more caution.

How often does the favourite win at each greyhound track?

Knowing how often favourites win at each track helps you weigh up a tip on the market leader. In graded racing, the favourite typically wins about a third of the time, but that varies noticeably from track to track. It's also higher in open races, where the gap in class between runners tends to be wider.

Who Writes Our Greyhound Racing Content?

This page is written by Darren Brett, who has more than 30 years' experience in racing and betting, including roles at The Jockey Club and SIS LIVE. He has been betting on greyhound racing for decades and, as manager of OLBG's Tipster Competition, oversees the tips posted across the site.

Darren Brett has worked in racing and betting for more than 30 years, with a background at The Jockey Club and SIS LIVE. FAQ

Greyhound Racing Tips FAQs

  • Yes. Every greyhound tip on this page is free. The tips are posted by OLBG members, and each race shows the most-tipped dog along with how many tips it has received and the comments behind the picks.

  • Start with the tips on this page, which show the most-tipped dog in each race along with the reasoning behind the picks, and compare them with your own view of the form.

    Early pace is one of the most important factors. Races are often decided by the run to the first bend, where crowding and bumping are common, so a dog that is quick out of the traps and likely to lead avoids most of the trouble. Check each dog's recent sectional (first-bend) times as well as its overall run times.

    Also consider whether a dog's running style suits its trap. A dog that likes to run close to the rail is better drawn inside than out wide. Look for dogs moving down in grade, or young, improving dogs that could still be ahead of their mark.

  • No single trap wins most often at every track. In 2025, Trap 1 was the best-performing trap at six tracks and Trap 6 at five, while Traps 2, 3 and 4 each came out on top elsewhere.

    With six runners, each trap would win around 16.7% of the time if the draw made no difference. The biggest biases in 2025 were Trap 6 at Harlow and Trap 1 at Towcester, both winning more than 23% of the time. Bias depends mainly on each track's layout and the run to the first bend, so check the track-by-track trap figures on this page before betting.

  • Yes. In 2025, the outright favourite won 35.8% of graded races across the tracks in our table, roughly one race in three. That varied from 31.1% at Kinsley to 42.5% at Valley.

    Favourites win more often in open races, where the gap in class between runners tends to be wider. In 2025, open-race favourites won 48.0% of the time overall, from 54.1% at Oxford down to 41.8% at Romford. You'll find the full track-by-track figures further up this page.

  • Yes. Sky Sports Racing shows selected greyhound meetings, mainly evening open racing and the big events. Almost every race at GBGB tracks is also streamed live through bookmaker websites and apps, where you'll usually need a funded account or a qualifying bet to watch.

  • OLBG's greyhound tips are win tips, so every selection on this page is a pick to win the race. The win market is the simplest greyhound bet: if your dog finishes first, your bet wins.

    Bookmakers also offer bets such as forecasts (first and second in the correct order) and tricasts (first, second and third in the correct order). Our greyhound betting guide explains these and other bet types in more detail.

  • In a handicap race, dogs of differing ability start from staggered positions to even out their chances. The fastest dog starts furthest back, known as running off "scratch", while slower dogs are given a head start. Each dog's starting allowance is shown on the racecard. Handicaps are much less common than graded races at British tracks.
